extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, journalists, and general newspaper readers
extracted.subtask_description: Coverage and commentary on press access, censorship, and clandestine/newssheet operations during wartime — i.e., norms for how newspapers/reporters should cover international conferences and how underground presses should operate under occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press access to international conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: “This policy denies reasonable access to original sources of information and progress of the forthcoming United Nations food conference.” (Roy A. Roberts / American Society of Newspaper Editors statement) — reporters should have reasonable access to original sources and to the progress of international conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without adequate information, sound public opinion cannot be formed; the government should not withhold or restrict information on the pretext that free inquiry might embarrass proceedings. Physical access to delegates should not be restricted; the policy should be abandoned. Exception: military information that would aid the enemy may be withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public right to know
rubrics_metrics.description: The government should not use voluntary censorship or restrict information that prevents the public from participating in public decisions: “The government should not withhold or restrict information on the food conference... The government should not use voluntary censor[ship]... The policy should be abandoned.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors argue that restricting access promotes distrust of government, stifles free inquiry, and prevents the continuous flow of full information needed for democracy. Coverage should enable citizens to form sound public opinion and participate in decisions; avoid secrecy that creates dangerous precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable scope of censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Military information that would aid the enemy may legitimately be withheld: “Military information is not involved. Press and public gladly withhold information that aid the enemy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between information whose disclosure would materially aid the enemy (which may be withheld) and information of public interest. Do not use the excuse of potential embarrassment to justify broad restrictions; censorship should be narrowly limited to genuine military/security risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational security for clandestine publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices used by underground/secret presses to survive occupation: keep ringleaders' names secret, shift publishing headquarters frequently, print simultaneously in several cities, buy necessary news stock on the black market, deliver door-to-door at night, use the blackout to advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decentralize production and distribution to avoid Gestapo detection; limit knowledge of leadership among helpers; change publishing locations often; accept high personal risk (arrest, torture, execution) and build procedures to protect personnel and continuity of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground press content priorities and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Underground papers should provide detailed reporting of allied progress, warn the population of enemy plots, and publish practical handbooks for resistance: e.g., “Vry Nederland regularly warns its readers’ against Nazi Gestapo plots... The editors also print special handbooks with suggestions on how to harass the Nazis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize actionable warnings (headlines like “Beware! Gestapo!”), morale-boosting accounts of allied strength, and practical guidance for resistance. Balance usefulness of guidance with operational security; expect censorship/retaliation but persist because the press can be a potent anti-occupation weapon.
